pages.seoTitle: Rabina Maharjan, architect in Patan: brick houses and courtyards
pages.seoDescription: Architect in Nag Bahal, Patan. New brick houses, courtyard restorations and small public buildings across the Kathmandu valley, drawn by hand first.

props.title: Brick houses that keep cool in Jestha and hold the sun in Poush
props.text: I design homes, courtyards and small public buildings in the Kathmandu valley, and repair the old ones. Local brick, deep eaves and rooms that face the right way.

props.intro: Built between 2076 and 2081. Every one is lived in.

items.title: House for two generations, Bungamati
items.text: Parents on the ground floor, a son’s family above, one kitchen between them. The glass-block stair lights both floors without a single west window.

props.heading: A one-architect studio, on purpose
props.body:
I work with one assistant and a model-maker, so the person who walks your plot is the one who draws every sheet and signs the naksa. That limits me to about six projects a year.

Most clients are families building on inherited land: a narrow plot in Kirtipur, a field in Bungamati, a crumbling house in a Patan bahal that three brothers want to share. The brief is usually more about the people than the building. That is where I like to start.

props.heading: One house, up close
props.intro: What the photograph does not tell you.

image.alt: A brick house with a glass-block wall and tall windows

points.title: The glass-block wall
points.text: Light for the stair, and no view into it from the lane.

points.title: Tall windows on the north
points.text: Even daylight for the rooms people work in, and no glare after lunch.

points.title: Brick from a kiln in Bhaktapur
points.text: Laid in lime mortar, so the wall can breathe and be repaired.

props.quote: A good house in the valley is not complicated. Face south, keep the west wall solid, make the eaves deep enough for Asar, and leave somewhere to sit outside.
props.name: Rabina Maharjan

props.heading: What I can do for you
props.intro: Fees are per square foot of finished floor, excluding VAT. Every project starts with a free first meeting.

items.title: New house, full design
items.text: Concept, design, approval drawings, working drawings and site visits during the build.

items.title: Naksa pass drawings only
items.text: For a design you already have. Drawings to your municipality’s rules, and I follow the file through approval.

items.title: Restoration of an old house
items.text: Measured survey, structural check with our engineer, and a repair plan that keeps what can be kept. Repair drawings are priced after the survey.

items.title: Site visits
items.text: For houses I did not design, when you want a second pair of eyes on the contractor. Two hours minimum.

items.q: Do you work outside the valley?
items.a: Sometimes, for a house or a school in Kavre, Nuwakot or Dhading. Travel is billed at cost and site visits are fewer, so we plan them carefully.
No. I help you choose a contractor, check their prices against my estimate and visit the site at every stage. Keeping design and building separate protects you.

items.q: What will the house cost to build?
items.a: In 2083, a well-built brick house in the valley costs roughly Rs 5,500 to 7,500 per square foot, depending on finishes. I give you an estimate at the design stage and update it before you sign with a builder.
Probably not. The Kirtipur house sits on a 22-foot frontage. Bring the lalpurja and the plot map and we will see what the bylaws allow.

props.title: Building on family land next year?
props.text: Come in for an hour, bring the plot map and your list of who will live there. The first meeting is free.

props.text: Built work from the last six years. Owners are happy to show visitors around two of the houses; ask and I will arrange it.

image.alt: The brick gable and deep timber eave of the Bungamati house against a blue sky

items.title: House for two generations, Bungamati, 2080
items.text: Brief: two households, one kitchen, a garden for vegetables and a parking space that does not look like a garage. The house sits on the north edge of the plot so the garden gets the winter sun. Walls are 14-inch brick from a kiln in Harisiddhi; the eaves project three feet to keep the monsoon off the windows. Built for Rs 1.9 crore over 14 months.

image.alt: The Nag Bahal courtyard with its repaired timber balconies and a tree

items.title: Chhen in Nag Bahal, 2079
items.text: Three brothers inherited one house and one courtyard, badly cracked after 2072. We rebuilt the back wall, tied the floors with timber bands, replaced the roof in jhingati tiles and gave each family its own stair and bathroom. Every carved window went back where it came from.

image.alt: A slim steel bridge crossing the brick light well of the Kirtipur house

items.title: Light-well house, Kirtipur, 2081
items.text: On a 22-foot frontage, the rooms turn inward to a planted light well. A steel bridge joins the front and back bedrooms on the upper floor, and the stair doubles as a bookshelf.

image.alt: Brick columns and long windows in the Khokana reading hall

items.title: Reading hall, Khokana
items.text: Forty seats, no fans needed. Built with the ward office and village masons.

props.text: One fee for the whole design, paid in five parts as the work is done. No percentage of the building cost, so I never gain from making it bigger.

props.heading: What is not in the fee

items.title: Municipal fees
items.text: Paid by you directly at the ward and municipality. I tell you the amounts before we file.

items.title: Soil test
items.text: Needed for most houses over two floors. A lab in the valley charges about Rs 35,000.

items.title: Travel outside the valley
items.text: Bus or jeep fare and a night’s stay, at cost.

items.title: Interior design
items.text: Built-in shelves and kitchens are included. Furniture and curtains are yours to choose.

items.q: Why per square foot and not a percentage?
items.a: A percentage of the building cost rewards the architect for making things bigger and more expensive. A fixed rate per square foot, agreed once the design is settled, does not.
You pay for the stages finished and keep every drawing and the model. Some families pause for a year to save; the design waits.

items.q: Can you work with our contractor?
items.a: Yes. I will check their prices against my estimate and tell you honestly if anything looks wrong.

props.title: Tell me about the plot
props.text: Size, road, who will live there and roughly what you can spend. I reply within two working days.

pages.title: About
pages.seoTitle: About Rabina Maharjan: training, practice and the studio team
pages.seoDescription: Architect trained at Pulchowk Campus, restoration work in Patan and Bhaktapur, her own studio in Nag Bahal since 2012. CV, team and teaching.

props.title: I grew up in a Patan courtyard. I still work in one.
props.text: Twenty years of drawing houses, four of them spent repairing old ones after the earthquake. The studio is on the first floor of a house in Nag Bahal, above a tailor.

image.alt: Rabina Maharjan in her studio

props.heading: Why brick, still
props.body:
The valley has built in fired brick for a thousand years because it works here: it is made from the ground you stand on, it breathes through the monsoon and it stores the winter sun. Concrete frames are not wrong, but they are often used where they are not needed.

I use concrete where it earns its place, in bands and slabs, and brick for everything the hand touches. The result costs about the same, lasts longer and ages well.
